concepts.title: Bill of Rights and Why Constitutions Need One

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bill of Rights and Why Constitutions Need One' refers to.
questions.a: A bill of rights is the part of a constitution that lists what the state may never do to individuals and what it must secure for them. It converts moral claims into enforceable entitlements, places limits even on elected majorities, and gives citizens legal weapons -- courts -- rather than appeals to goodwill.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bill of Rights and Why Constitutions Need One'.
questions.a: Rights written as law and guarded by courts survive the change of governments and moods.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Bill of Rights and Why Constitutions Need One' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: keps202.txt lines 15-110 (introduction, bill of rights, why rights need constitutional status, rights and the limits of majorities))

concepts.title: The Six Fundamental Rights: An Overview

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Six Fundamental Rights: An Overview' refers to.
questions.a: Part III of the Constitution lists six fundamental rights: equality (Articles 14-18), freedom (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), freedom of religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights of minorities (29-30), and constitutional remedies (32). Together they cover the citizen's public, personal and group life.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Six Fundamental Rights: An Overview'.
questions.a: Six rights, one shield -- equality, freedom, anti-exploitation, religion, minority culture, and the remedy that unlocks the rest.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Six Fundamental Rights: An Overview' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps202.txt lines 110-220 (list of fundamental rights in part three, equality rights, right to freedom, right against exploitation, religious and cultural rights, remedies))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rights and Reasonable Restrictions' refers to.
questions.a: Indian fundamental rights are not absolute: the Constitution itself allows reasonable restrictions -- for public order, decency, health, sovereignty and the rights of others. A restriction is valid only if imposed by law, for a listed purpose, and proportionate; otherwise courts strike it down as an unconstitutional invasion.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rights and Reasonable Restrictions'.
questions.a: Rights come with rule-of-law brakes -- limits must be lawful, listed and proportionate, not arbitrary.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Rights and Reasonable Restrictions' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps202.txt lines 220-330 (reasonable restrictions on rights, limits on freedom of speech and assembly, judicial review of restrictions))

concepts.title: Directive Principles and Their Relation to Rights

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Directive Principles and Their Relation to Rights' refers to.
questions.a: Part IV carries directive principles -- instructions to the state to fight inequality, secure livelihoods, protect environment and workers, and promote village self-government. They are non-justiciable, yet they complete Part III: rights guard the individual from the state, directives command the state to build conditions where those rights mean something.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Directive Principles and Their Relation to Rights'.
questions.a: Rights stop the state from harming; directives push the state to help -- two halves of one constitutional vision.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Directive Principles and Their Relation to Rights' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.4 (source: keps202.txt lines 330-430 (directive principles of state policy, their non-justiciability, relation with fundamental rights, equal pay, environment, village panchayats))
